summary:
AstroSentinel is an offline-first health monitoring system for astronauts on deep-space missions. At Mars, a message to Earth takes up to 22 minutes each way, and solar conjunction can cut the link for about two weeks, so a medical emergency cannot wait for Houston. AstroSentinel moves medical decision support on board.

It tracks each crew member’s vital signs and biomarkers against their own preflight baseline. It turns them into an explainable 0–100 risk score, where every point is traced to a biomarker, and recommends actions such as moving to the storm shelter. The model follows a real scientific chain: space radiation, then disruption of endothelial Notch signaling, then vascular and blood-brain-barrier vulnerability, plus the microgravity eye syndrome SANS.

The crew console is a first-person EVA helmet HUD that projects vital signs, suit life support and radiation alerts onto the visor. Health digests are stored and forwarded with the real light-time delay, and Mission Control sees only what has actually arrived.

The result is decisions in seconds instead of up to 44 minutes, with full transparency for the crew medical officer.
details:
What it does
At Mars, a radio message needs 3 to 22 minutes each way, and during solar conjunction the link can drop for about two weeks. A medical emergency cannot wait 44 minutes for Houston. AstroSentinel moves health monitoring on board. It watches each astronaut’s vital signs and biomarkers, calculates risk locally, recommends actions, and syncs with Earth only when the link allows.

How it works

  • Explainable risk engine. Each biomarker becomes a z-score against the astronaut’s own preflight baseline: Notch Disruption Index, radiation dose, intraocular pressure and blood-brain-barrier permeability. These are combined into a 0–100 score: Nominal, Watch or Alert. Every point traces back to a specific biomarker, so there is no black box.
  • Science-based model. We follow one chain: space radiation → endothelial Notch signaling disruption (Jag2, Notch4) → weaker vessels and blood-brain barrier. We also track SANS, the microgravity eye syndrome, through intraocular pressure.
  • Delay-tolerant sync. Health digests are created on board. During loss of signal they are queued, then sent with the real scaled light-time delay. Mission Control sees only what has actually arrived. A live “Deep-Space Link” visualiser shows packets crossing between Mars and Earth.
  • First-person EVA helmet HUD. The crew console is seen from inside the astronaut’s helmet. Vital signs, suit life support (O₂, CO₂, pressure, battery, temperature, water), radiation and the next checklist action are projected onto the visor, with Mars in front of you. In a solar particle event the Sun flares, protons stream past the visor and the HUD raises a master alarm.
  • Hands-free voice copilot, 72-hour what-if radiation forecast, on-board checklist, and a Mission Control view with crew status, 14-day trends, a reply uplink and a printable report.

Benefits and impact
The crew gets a decision in seconds instead of waiting up to 44 minutes for a round trip to Earth. Explainable scores build trust, and personal baselines catch problems that population averages miss. Because dose is treated as a driver, the crew can shelter before biomarkers move. The same approach can help remote clinics, polar stations and submarines where specialists are far away.

Tools and technologies

  • Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, Recharts.
  • Native browser APIs only: Server-Sent Events, Canvas 2D (including a real-time spherical projection of a Mars texture), Web Audio, Web Speech recognition and synthesis.
  • No database and no external services, so the system runs fully offline.
  • Visual media: NASA SDO solar flare footage, and planet textures from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0, based on NASA data).

Creativity
We turned an abstract idea, the communication delay, into something you can see and feel. You literally look through the astronaut’s visor, and you watch data packets fly across space at the speed of light, piling up while the link is lost.

What our team considered
Real Mars light-time and solar conjunction, astronauts’ limited attention and hands-free use, explainability for crew medical officers, and accessibility (screen-reader labels, reduced-motion support).

Honesty statement: all values are synthetic, calibrated to plausible ranges informed by NASA open science resources (NASA OSDR/GeneLab, the NASA Twins Study, the Life Sciences Data Archive). AstroSentinel is decision support, not a diagnosis; a human crew medical officer confirms every action.
